provenance.other: “make a sure covenant” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, Nehemiah 9:38, and it is the KJV's only covenant that is ratified by writing down the names of the people who enter it: 'we make a sure covenant, and write it; and our princes, Levites, and priests, seal unto it', followed in Nehemiah 10:1-27 by the list of names.
provenance.significance: Mosiah 6:1-6 runs the Nehemiah 9-10 sequence in Nehemiah's order and this is its first term. A public reading of the law to an assembled people (Nehemiah 8) → a covenant sealed by name (9:38-10:27) → an oath binding them to walk in God's law and observe his commandments, judgments and statutes (10:29) → Mosiah 6:1, names taken; 6:3, 'the oath which they had made'; 6:6, walking, observing, keeping. The Book of Mormon's one narrative of a written covenant roll is built on the Bible's one narrative of a written covenant roll, and the borrowing is structural rather than verbal, which is why it is filed at moderate and conceptual.

6:1.note: 'That he should take the names of all those who had entered into a covenant with God, to keep his commandments.' No clause is reproduced. What is reproduced is a procedure the KJV describes once — a covenant made sure by recording who is in it — and the three following verses go on reproducing it. The machine stream proposed Ezekiel 16:8 and Jeremiah 34:10 for 'entered into a covenant', which is the KJV's ordinary phrase; the distinctive act here is the taking of names, and only Nehemiah has it.
6:1.text: And because of all this we make a sure covenant, and write it; and our princes, Levites, and priests, seal unto it.

provenance.other: “nameth the name of Christ” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Timothy 2:19, and so does “them that are his”. 'The name of Christ' as such occurs in two verses, 2 Timothy 2:19 and 1 Peter 4:14, but 1 Peter's is about being reproached for it, not taking it upon oneself.
provenance.significance: This is the strongest single piece of evidence in the three chapters and it is not at the verse where the words are. 2 Timothy 2:19 holds three things in twenty-eight words: a seal, the sentence 'The Lord knoweth them that are his', and naming the name of Christ. Mosiah 5:13-15 and 6:2 hold the same three, in the same order and across four verses — 5:13 asks how a man can know a master he has not served, 5:15 asks that Christ 'may seal you his', and 6:2 says every soul 'had taken upon them the name of Christ'. 'Seal', 'his', and 'the name of Christ' are all in one KJV verse and all in one stretch of Benjamin's conclusion. The suppressed half is Paul's condition, 'depart from iniquity', which Mosiah 5:11 has already supplied as the exception under which the name is blotted out.

6:2.note: 'There was not one soul, except it were little children, but what had entered into the covenant, and had taken upon them the name of Christ.' Taken alone the phrase is shared with two KJV verses and the link would be moderate at best. Taken with 5:15's 'seal you his' — where 'them that are his' is a KJV singleton at the same verse that names the name of Christ — the coincidence stops being a coincidence. Recorded at 6:2 because that is where the borrowed words stand; the argument is made across 5:13-6:2 and the recurrence field carries it.
6:2.text: Nevertheless the foundation of God standeth sure, having this seal, The Lord knoweth them that are his. And, Let every one that nameth the name of Christ depart from iniquity.

provenance.other: “appointed him to be ruler” and “king in my stead” both occur in exactly one KJV verse, and it is the same verse, 1 Kings 1:35 — David installing Solomon. “king over his people” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Samuel 15:1, Samuel anointing Saul. “charged Solomon” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 2:1.
provenance.significance: Benjamin's succession is Solomon's. 1 Kings 1:35 makes the heir both ruler and king in one sentence, which is the pairing Mosiah 6:3 keeps — 'a ruler and a king over his people' — and 1 Kings 2:1-3 has the dying father charging his son, which is Mosiah 6:3's 'given him all the charges concerning the kingdom' and 6:5's death two verses later. The Book of Mormon has taken the Davidic transfer whole: appointment, double title, charge, death, and then at 6:6 the son walking in the ways of the Lord, which is 1 Kings 2:3's own next clause.

6:3.note: 'Had consecrated his son Mosiah, to be a ruler and a king over his people, and had given him all the charges concerning the kingdom.' The double title is the tell. The KJV appoints a man ruler and calls him king in one breath exactly once, and that once is the verse where a king hands his throne to his son before dying. 'Over his people' comes from the other royal installation, Saul's. The machine stream's best proposal here was Acts 7:35's 'to be a ruler and a', six words — and Acts's next word is 'deliverer', Moses and not a king. Read the whole candidate verse.
6:3.text: Then ye shall come up after him, that he may come and sit upon my throne; for he shall be king in my stead: and I have appointed him to be ruler over Israel and over Judah.

provenance.other: “departed every one to his house” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 6:19, the dismissal of the assembly after David brings up the ark. 1 Kings 8:66 is the same act at the end of Solomon's temple dedication — 'he sent the people away … and they went unto their tents'.
provenance.significance: The KJV has two great royal assemblies that end with the king sending the people home, and they are David's and Solomon's — the same two reigns this chapter has been quoting since 6:3. Mosiah 6:3's dismissal formula falls exactly where 1 Kings 8:66's does, at the close of a multi-day gathering built around a king, a sacrifice and a covenant, and the phrase it uses is 2 Samuel 6:19's.

6:3.note: 'He dismissed the multitude, and they returned, every one according to their families, to their own houses.' The Book of Mormon inserts 'according to their families', which is neither source's, and keeps the rest. Filed at moderate as an echo because dismissing an assembly is a thing narratives have to say and the KJV's ways of saying it are few; what raises it above nothing is that the two KJV verses which say it this way are the two royal assemblies this chapter is already imitating.
6:3.text: And he dealt among all the people, even among the whole multitude of Israel, as well to the women as men, to every one a cake of bread, and a good piece of flesh, and a flagon of wine. So all the people departed every one to his house.

provenance.other: “thirty years old when he began to reign” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Samuel 5:4 — David. “to reign in his stead” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Chronicles 1:8, and it is Solomon's own account of his accession: 'thou hast shewed great mercy unto David my father, and hast made me to reign in his stead.' The KJV's ordinary regnal formula is the past 'reigned in his stead' (1 Kings 11:43 and dozens more); the infinitive is Solomon's alone.
provenance.significance: Two verses, two kings, one succession. Mosiah begins to reign at the age at which David began to reign, in the words in which Solomon described succeeding David. Neither datum is required by the narrative — the Book of Mormon supplies a regnal age here and nowhere else in the chapter — and the chronological note that follows ('four hundred and seventy-six years from the time that Lehi left Jerusalem') is itself a Kings-style synchronism. This verse is where the Davidic frame of 6:3-6 becomes arithmetic.

6:4.note: 'And Mosiah began to reign in his father's stead. And he began to reign in the thirtieth year of his age.' The two clauses are the two KJV singletons, in reverse order to their sources. The n-gram stream proposed 2 Kings 15:13 for the first and Ezekiel 1:1 for the second, both of which share the frame and neither of which has the age and the accession together; the verse that has both is David's.
6:4.text: David was thirty years old when he began to reign, and he reigned forty years.

provenance.other: “his judgments and his statutes” occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Deuteronomy 8:11 and Nehemiah 10:29. Deuteronomy has 'his commandments, and his judgments, and his statutes' inside a warning against forgetting; Nehemiah has walking, observing, commandments, judgments and statutes, in that order, inside an oath.
provenance.significance: The mediation is between two Old Testament verses rather than between Testaments, and the deciding evidence is the verb and the frame. Both candidates list judgments and statutes in that order, and only Nehemiah supplies 'walk' and 'observe', which are Mosiah 6:6's two other verbs. Nehemiah also supplies the setting: 10:29 is the oath sworn by the people whose names were sealed in 10:1-27, which is Mosiah 6:1's list, and it is 'the oath which they had made' that Mosiah 6:3 says the priests are appointed to stir the people up in remembrance of. The chapter's evaluation of Mosiah's reign is written in the vocabulary of the covenant his people had just signed.

6:6.note: 'Did walk in the ways of the Lord, and did observe his judgments, and his statutes, and did keep his commandments.' Five of Nehemiah 10:29's terms in Nehemiah's sequence. The machine stream ranked Deuteronomy 8:11 and Nehemiah 10:29 within a hundredth of each other, which is a fair reading of the shared string and a poor reading of the evidence: Deuteronomy's verse is a prohibition ('Beware that thou forget not'), and it has no 'walk' and no 'observe'.
6:6.text: They clave to their brethren, their nobles, and entered into a curse, and into an oath, to walk in God’s law, which was given by Moses the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the LORD our Lord, and his judgments and his statutes;

provenance.other: “walk in his ways to keep his statutes” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 1 Kings 2:3, which is David's dying charge to Solomon: 'keep the charge of the LORD thy God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments'.
provenance.significance: This is the other half of a link the chapter makes twice. Nehemiah 10:29 supplies the covenant-oath vocabulary; 1 Kings 2:3 supplies the same four nouns in a father's charge to a son who is about to reign — which is what Mosiah 6:3 has just narrated in 1 Kings 1:35's words. Read with 6:3 and 6:4, the sequence is David's exactly: appoint him ruler and king, charge him, die, and let the son walk in the ways of the Lord. The Book of Mormon has not chosen between its two sources and neither should the catalogue; both are registered, with Nehemiah carrying the verbs and Kings carrying the situation.

6:6.note: 'Did walk in the ways of the Lord, and did observe his judgments, and his statutes, and did keep his commandments in all things whatsoever he commanded him.' 1 Kings 2:3 is the KJV's only sentence pairing walking in his ways with keeping his statutes, and it stands two verses after 'he charged Solomon his son' — the charge Mosiah 6:3 says Benjamin gave. Filed at moderate rather than high because Nehemiah 10:29 accounts for the wording better and because a double attribution weakens each; the reason to keep it is that no reading of 6:3-6 as a whole works without it.
6:6.text: And keep the charge of the LORD thy God, to walk in his ways, to keep his statutes, and his commandments, and his judgments, and his testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses, that thou mayest prosper in all that thou doest, and whithersoever thou turnest thyself:

provenance.other: 'Burdensome' occurs in five KJV verses. One is Zechariah's burdensome stone; the other four are Paul refusing to be a charge on a congregation (2 Corinthians 11:9, 12:13, 12:14, 1 Thessalonians 2:6). “not be burdensome to you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, 2 Corinthians 12:14. 2 Thessalonians 3:8 gives the practice behind the principle — “chargeable to any of you” occurs in exactly one KJV verse, and it is that one: 'wrought with labour and travail night and day, that we might not be chargeable to any of you'. The 1830 reads 'burthensome', an archaic spelling that is not the KJV's; 1920 corrected it to the KJV's 'burdensome'.
provenance.significance: Mosiah's tilling is a Pauline argument in a king's mouth. The one thing the King James Bible says about not being burdensome is said by an apostle who supported himself with his hands so that his ministry would cost nothing, and Mosiah works the earth himself for exactly that reason. Note the direction of the 1830-to-1920 change: the first edition's 'burthensome' obscures the borrowing and the later correction restores it, so the modern text shows the KJV more plainly than the earliest one does — the reverse of the usual pattern in this catalogue.

6:7.note: 'That thereby he might not become burthensome to his people.' The word carries the link and it is a word the KJV reserves almost entirely to one Pauline argument. What secures it is the rationale, which is Paul's and not a king's: 2 Corinthians 12:14 refuses support on the ground that 'the children ought not to lay up for the parents, but the parents for the children', and 2 Thessalonians 3:8 refuses it by working night and day. Mosiah's fields are the same refusal. Filed at moderate because the shared vocabulary is one word and the argument does the rest.
6:7.text: Behold, the third time I am ready to come to you; and I will not be burdensome to you: for I seek not yours but you: for the children ought not to lay up for the parents, but the parents for the children.
